title: I've added something important about memory.
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Reading Lisa Genova's book on memory, Skelton finds it confirms that repeated experiences make things sticky, and that memory is not a separate thing but the result of stickiness spread across the brain. What he takes from it that is new is that attention must come first, because repetition can only strengthen a memory that attention has created. He links this to clickbait, to the pull of charismatic people, and to students choosing subjects for the teacher rather than the subject. He revisits his career, from a first-year classroom where students were attentive but not learning to the International Primary Curriculum's Entry Point, which was designed purely to seize attention before a unit began. He ends with questions about how to win the attention of students, colleagues, parents and boards.
points: Attention precedes repeated experience: without it no memory is formed to strengthen.
Clickbait and charisma both work by capturing attention, which explains why headlines hook us and why students gravitate to certain teachers.
Gaining attention is not enough, since his early mentor's remark showed that attentive students are only the first step before learning is actually produced.
An Entry Point activity, such as the mysterious spacemen and rocket in a playground, is designed purely to ignite curiosity before formal learning starts.
Attention driven only by exams has a short shelf life, whereas interest sparked by a teacher's approach can last.
quotes: Repetition definitely fortifies memory, but first you have to create a memory to strengthen and, without attention, this doesn’t happen.

It makes sense to me - sort of Duh!, actually - that initial attention matters a great deal at the beginning of making things sticky. If I don’t pay attention to the political/sport/ culture pages of my newspaper, magazine or social media that I am looking at, it’s obvious that the process of ‘making sticky’ something isn’t going to begin if I haven’t kicked the whole thing off by being attentive.

Highlighting attention explains why clickbait - those headlines that are designed to make us click further into a social media story and, therefor across more advertisements - is so powerful and important.

Charisma also helps to explain why children and students like some teachers more than others and why, even quite late into their school careers, a significant number of students report that they elect to take subjects based on the attraction of their teacher rather than the subject. They choose the subjects taught by the people who gain their attention.

If the students weren’t engaged - weren’t paying attention - the chances of learning whatever was planned were reduced. As Lisa Genova said, attention and engagement is the necessary beginning of the learning process as well as desirable outcomes.

What Lisa Genova makes clear is that this attention grabbing activity wasn’t just a pleasing series of fun moments one Monday in school; it was the necessary foundational starting point on which upcoming repeated experiences about space, planetary behaviour and more would make more sense and be more likely to be made sticky.

Attention is the beginning of making things meaningful; it’s the door that lets in enjoyment of the repeated experiences that are so essential to learning; it’s the start of laying down memories and making things sticky.
